mainEntity.name: How is a penetration test different from a security scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: An automated scan looks for known patterns. A manual penetration test checks which findings are actually exploitable and also tests the app's own logic (such as permissions and payments). We use automated tools during testing too, but we do not hand over their raw output.
A public standard for scoring vulnerability severity, from 0 to 10. It helps your team decide what to fix first.
Once, we test the findings we reported again to see whether they are fixed. New parts or other changes to the system need a new test.

Before any testing, three documents are signed

items: Written scope: exactly which domains, apps, APIs and accounts are tested and which are not, in what time window and with which methods.
Letter of Authorisation: the legal owner of the system grants permission to test, in writing.
Non-disclosure agreement (NDA): findings and any data seen during testing stay confidential.

blocks.html: Without all three, we do not test anything, not even a short trial.
Penetration testing
Know where your system is open before an attacker finds it: manual testing under a signed scope, a scored report, and a retest after the fixes.
Problem

If you run a web app or an API that processes user data or payments, the question is not whether you have vulnerabilities. The question is which ones are actually exploitable, and what someone reaches if they get through.

An automated scan does not answer that: it produces a long list of warnings, half of which do not matter. And on the other side, a report that never says what was out of scope gives false comfort. Teams usually end up either buried under unprioritised warnings, or holding a report that says secure without it being clear what was ever tested.

We test manually, under a scope signed before we start, with an authorisation letter and an NDA alongside it. Every finding is reported with a CVSS score, evidence, impact, and a fix, and retesting the findings is included in the price. And we say it plainly from the start: no test proves complete security, and we do not write such certificates.
Who it is for

items: Teams with a web app or API that handles user data, payments or sensitive information.
Startups whose customers or partners ask for a security test report before signing.
Teams that want a sensitive feature (login, payments, admin panel) tested before launch.

blocks.html: Who it is not for

items: If you do not own the system and do not have the owner's written authorisation.
If you want a "fully secure" or "zero vulnerabilities" certificate. No test proves that, and we do not write it.
If you only want an automated scanner run and its raw output handed over.
If you need social engineering, physical, or internal network infrastructure testing.

blocks.html: Approach

items: Scope. Input: a conversation about the system and its risks. Output: signed written scope, Letter of Authorisation and NDA. Owner: you and dadmor.

Test. Input: the signed scope and test accounts. Output: findings with evidence. Method: PTES for structure, OWASP WSTG for web testing, and the OWASP Top 10 and API Security Top 10 where relevant. Owner: dadmor.
Report. Input: the findings. Output: an executive report and a technical report; each finding with a CVSS score, evidence, impact and remediation. Owner: dadmor.
Fix. Input: the report. Output: fixes in your system. Owner: your team.
Retest. Input: the fixes you report. Output: one retest of the reported findings and an updated status report. Owner: dadmor, within the window written in the scope.

blocks.html: Deliverables
Scope and timeline factors

items: What changes the size of the work: number of apps, APIs and endpoints, number of user roles (guest, user, admin), and business logic that must be tested (payments, permissions).
What you supply: a test environment or permission to test production, test accounts for each role, one technical contact, and the three signed documents.
What delays projects: authorisation signed late, test accounts that do not work, and an environment that changes mid-test.

blocks.html: Effort band

items: A fixed-scope proposal after the scoping conversation only. One retest of the reported findings is included.

blocks.html: Limits and risks

items: A penetration test checks what was in scope, at a point in time. Anything outside the scope, and any change after the test, was not checked, and the report says so.
Not finding a vulnerability means this test did not find it, not that none exists.
Testing production can risk downtime or data changes; high-risk techniques run only with written approval and at an agreed time.
Fixing the vulnerabilities is your team's work unless it is scoped separately.
